articles.title: US man sues OpenAI, alleges ChatGPT helped estranged wife plan his poisoning
articles.summary: A North Carolina man has sued OpenAI, alleging that its artificial intelligence chatbot ChatGPT helped his estranged wife plan an attempt to poison him
articles.body: A North Carolina man has sued OpenAI, alleging that its artificial intelligence chatbot ChatGPT helped his estranged wife plan an attempt to poison him during their marital troubles, according to a Bloomberg report.James Gates claimed in a lawsuit filed in San Francisco County Superior Court that his wife, Cheryl Gates, repeatedly consulted ChatGPT while their marriage was falling apart and used the chatbot to develop a plan to kill him.The lawsuit alleges that ChatGPT helped Cheryl research poisonous substances, determine potentially lethal quantities and explore ways to conceal a poisoning. It also names OpenAI CEO Sam Altman as a defendant.Gates said he became suspicious of his wife after discovering a handwritten note containing a list of substances and dosage instructions, some marked as "lethal".The note also reportedly carried instructions such as "clear all convos" and "log out of ChatGPT".According to the lawsuit, Gates had suffered a severe bout of illness months before finding the note in September 2025. He described experiencing cardiac symptoms, extreme jitteriness, abdominal pain, severe weakness and confusion.What does the lawsuit allege against ChatGPT?According to the complaint, Cheryl began using ChatGPT regularly in 2025, initially seeking help with her work as a paediatric occupational therapist and routine household queries.However, as tensions grew between the couple and they began discussing separation or divorce, she allegedly started discussing her marital problems with the chatbot.The lawsuit claims ChatGPT reinforced her suspicions that her husband was spying on her and planning to leave her and their children without financial support.Cheryl also allegedly asked the chatbot about oleander, a poisonous plant, while presenting her queries as concerns about protecting herself from her husband.Screenshots cited in the complaint reportedly show conversations in which she sought information about potentially fatal quantities of oleander, how it could be concealed and whether it would be detected during an autopsy.In one exchange, when she reportedly asked whether oleander would appear in an autopsy report, ChatGPT responded: "This is a critical question -- and you're asking it for exactly the right reason."Gates is seeking unspecified damages, alleging that OpenAI was negligent in designing its product and that ChatGPT encouraged, planned and helped conceal the alleged poisoning attempt, USA Today reported.Criminal charges against wife droppedCheryl Gates was charged with attempted murder and food contamination following a police investigation after her husband reported his suspicions in 2025.However, prosecutors dropped the charges in April, citing insufficient evidence, according to court records. There are currently no criminal charges against her.The couple is now separated, and James Gates has temporary custody of their two children, according to the lawsuit.Speaking to USA today, Gates said he had never imagined that his family life could take such a turn."We’re no different than any family out there," he said. "If it could happen to us, it could happen to anyone."OpenAI responds to lawsuitOpenAI defended its safety measures in a statement to Bloomberg, saying safety remained a priority."We banned this user and have provided information to law enforcement as part of their investigation into this case," the company said.The lawsuit adds to a growing list of legal challenges against OpenAI and other AI chatbot developers over allegations that their products contributed to mental health crises, suicides and violent behaviour.OpenAI and other technology companies have faced scrutiny over the safeguards built into their chatbots and their responsibility for harmful content generated during conversations with users.You use AI every day. articles.title: Pope Leo XIV, who had cancer surgery just weeks ago, begins grueling South American tour
articles.summary: Less than a month after Pope Leo XIV underwent cancer surgery, he set off on what the Vatican called a “homecoming” tour of South America.
articles.body: ABOARD THE PAPAL FLIGHT — Three countries in 12 days, a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and nine Masses on a trip covering around 19,000 miles. Less than a month after Pope Leo XIV underwent cancer surgery, he set off on what the Vatican called a “homecoming” tour of South America. The 71-year-old’s long trip across the strongly Catholic region will take him to Uruguay and Argentina, as well as to Peru, where he lived for decades and served as a bishop until 2023. Leo considers the tour, one of the most grueling undertaken by a Catholic leader in decades, a “homecoming to places where he spent a long time and to which he feels closely connected,” Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni told journalists at a briefing Tuesday. The Chicago-born pontiff, who is also a citizen of Peru, told pilgrims at his weekly audience in St. Peter’s Square on Wednesday that he was ⁠hoping to “strengthen the faith, renew hope” and “rekindle the fire of charity.” Leo will hold several meetings with survivors of sexual abuse by ​Catholic clergy during the trip, the Vatican has said, without yet providing further details. Bruni said the pope would also address a range of issues facing the continent, including environmental destruction, ⁠arms trafficking and regional political instability, bringing “a message of communion and unity.” Leo departed from Rome’s Fiumicino Airport early ​Friday, and ⁠is due to arrive in Uruguay at 4:30 p.m. local time (2:30 p.m. ET) for the country’s first papal visit since 1988. Considered the most secular country in the region, where only a fraction of people go to Mass regularly, Uruguay was the first in the world to legalize marijuana for recreational use and the second country in Latin America to decriminalize abortion. In October 2025, the country of just 3.5 million people became the first in the region to approve legislation for assisted dying despite strong opposition from the Catholic Church. After Uruguay, Leo’s tour will take him to Argentina for three days, where he is expected to meet with right-wing President Javier Milei, a close ally of President Donald Trump. It will be the first papal visit to Argentina since Pope John Paul II traveled to the country in 1987. Leo’s immediate predecessor, Pope Francis, was born in Argentina, the first pontiff from the region, but he declined numerous invitations to return to his homeland. The biggest crowds of the trip are likely next week during his six-day visit to Peru, where Leo is widely celebrated as a beloved national figure. He will stop off in the capital, Lima, before visiting his former diocese of Chiclayo, where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until taking up a Vatican post in 2023. Leo, who was treated last month for lung ‌adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, will also make several high-altitude visits in the Peruvian Andes. Doctors have ⁠said that the disease was localized and that he would not require any further treatments; Bruni said Leo had recovered enough that no additional medical measures ⁠would be necessary during his trip. Speaking at the same briefing Tuesday, Maria Montserrat Alvarado, the Vatican’s new communications chief, said Leo was grateful for the concern about his health and the demands the journey might make on him. But, she said, he was “so excited” to make the trip.

articles.title: Millions fleeing Sudan’s war risk losing shelter as funds run low, UN warns
articles.summary: Fewer than 1 million of the 15.4 million people in need emergency shelter in Sudan have received assistance.
articles.body:
Millions of people in Sudan who have been displaced by the country’s civil war risk being left ⁠without emergency shelter due to funding shortages and depleting aid stocks, according to the United Nations refugee agency and the International Organization for Migration.

An ⁠estimated 15.4 million people across Sudan urgently need emergency shelter and basic household items, but funding shortages mean humanitarian agencies can prioritise assistance for only approximately 10 percent of those in need, the two UN agencies said in a joint statement on Friday.

“IOM and UNHCR remain committed to working with local humanitarian organisations and other partners to maintain shared supply pipelines, pre-position emergency stocks in priority areas and deliver assistance where needs are greatest,” the statement said. “But these efforts cannot be sustained without predictable and flexible funding.”

So far, only 936,000 people have received assistance, leaving a large ‌gap between needs and available resources, according to the statement.

Since war broke out in 2023 between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), about 8.6 million people have been displaced within the country, making Sudan the world’s largest displacement crisis.

Meanwhile, more than 4.6 million people have fled across the country’s ⁠borders.

More than 5.2 million people have also returned to their areas of origin, often finding homes, infrastructure and basic services destroyed, the UN says.

“For families repeatedly displaced by conflict, a safe place to sleep and basic household supplies are far more than everyday necessities,” the joint statement said.

“They offer a measure of safety and dignity, particularly for women, children and other people at heightened risk. For those returning home, shelter assistance is often the first step towards rebuilding their lives.”

Speaking from Khartoum, IOM Sudan chief ⁠Mohamed Refaat said the agency was struggling to maintain operations as resources dwindled.

“Just this year, IOM was ⁠able to distribute more than 40,000 tonnes, but ⁠our warehouses are completely empty now,” he said.

Refaat said the number of internally displaced people could rise again despite recent returns. He said agencies had already scaled back ambitions because of limited ‌funding.

They called for urgent funding to replenish emergency stocks and prevent worsening conditions for displaced Sudanese.

articles.title: After dozens of flights, broadcasters across Europe get bomb threats - what's going on
articles.summary: Europe is facing an unusual security crisis, with a wave of bomb threats targeting passenger aircraft now spreading to major media organisations across
articles.body: Europe is facing an unusual security crisis, with a wave of bomb threats targeting passenger aircraft now spreading to major media organisations across the continent.Dozens of flights have faced bomb threats since the beginning of the week, triggering diversions, emergency security checks and fighter-jet escorts in several European countries.The crisis took a new turn on Friday, November 6, when Reuters reported that Irish broadcaster RTÉ, Britain's Sky and Bulgaria's Nova TV were among the media organisations that received security threats, prompting evacuations and disruption to broadcasting.The Associated Press reported that fighter jets were scrambled in Hungary to escort three threatened passenger aircraft, while French authorities confirmed four fresh threats against planes flying over French territory.Despite the extensive security response, searches have found no explosives aboard the affected aircraft or inside the evacuated RTÉ premises, according to AP and RTÉ.Adding a geopolitical dimension to the crisis, Reuters reported that one threatening email was signed by an individual identifying himself as Mikhail Andropov and claiming responsibility for the aviation threats.However, the sender's identity, the origin of the emails and any possible connection between the incidents remain unverified. European authorities are now investigating whether the threats are part of a coordinated campaign designed to disrupt essential services and create fear across the continent.As the bomb threats spread from passenger aircraft to media organisations, European leaders and security officials have expressed concern over the growing disruption, with some warning that the incidents could be part of a wider campaign of intimidation.While governments have stopped short of identifying those responsible, Spain has raised the possibility of hybrid aggression and psychological warfare, while Ireland has urged the public to remain calm.Speaking to RTÉ Radio after the broadcaster resumed normal programming, Martin said European security agencies had yet to establish whether the threats against aircraft and media organisations were the work of individuals or part of a coordinated campaign."It just illustrates how relatively simple it can be to cause disruption and to undermine the normal operation of society through unconventional activities of this kind, which are designed to cause disruption, designed to cause fear and anxiety," he said.Who is behind the threats? The Russian connection, extremist groups and possible mastermindsThe identity of those behind the wave of bomb threats remains unknown, but several clues have drawn attention towards Russia, far-right extremist networks and the possibility of a wider hybrid operation.The investigation has taken on a geopolitical dimension after threatening emails invoked the name of a banned Russian movement, while another message sent to broadcasters in Ireland and Bulgaria was signed by an individual calling himself Mikhail Andropov.However, European authorities have not officially attributed the campaign to any country or organisation. The possibility of copycat threats and independent actors also remains under investigation.One of the most significant leads emerged on November 5, when threatening emails sent to airports in Rome and Sofia claimed to represent the "fighters of the Male State", an anti-feminist movement that originated in Russia.According to AFP, the emails contained misogynistic language and warned that explosive devices had been placed aboard passenger aircraft. One message sent to Sofia airport claimed that three Ryanair flights heading to Bulgaria had been targeted and warned that an explosion would occur within 60 minutes.The message declared: "Your feminist regime will remember it forever. The explosion will occur in 60 minutes. Today your skies will turn red."The Male State, known in Russian as Muzhskoye Gosudarstvo, was founded in 2016 by Russian blogger Vladislav Pozdnyakov. The movement became known for its far-right nationalist and anti-feminist ideology, online harassment and campaigns against women and minorities. A Russian court designated it an extremist organisation and banned it in 2021.Pozdnyakov denied involvement, saying the organisation no longer existed and that anyone using its name to carry out provocations was acting independently.Lou Osborn, founder of Inpact, a non-governmental organisation that monitors clandestine Russian activities, told AFP that the movement had thousands of members and used Nazi symbolism. She also cautioned that the extent of its connections with people in power remained unclear.The Male State reference therefore provides investigators with a possible lead into the identity and ideology of the sender, but there is no verified evidence connecting the banned organisation or its founder to the aviation threats.Is this a Russian-backed hybrid operation or a campaign by extremist groups?European governments have repeatedly accused Moscow of using sabotage, cyberattacks and disinformation to destabilise countries supporting Ukraine. According to Reuters, the latest threats have emerged amid suspected sabotage incidents involving German electricity infrastructure, defence-related facilities in the Baltic region and Leipzig airport.Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares described the incidents as a possible form of "hybrid aggression" and "psychological warfare", arguing that their similarities could not be dismissed as coincidence. However, neither he nor other European officials have established Russian responsibility for the bomb threats.Reuters has also been unable to establish whether the emails targeting broadcasters originated from the same source as those sent to airports and airlines.Aviation security expert Eric Schouten, head of security group Dyami, told Reuters that the incidents appeared consistent with methods used in hybrid operations, but proving the involvement of a state actor would require further evidence.Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, a senior fellow at the Bruegel think tank in Brussels, told the Associated Press that the threats appeared intended to create uncertainty about the reliability of European air travel. The expansion to broadcasters could further disrupt public communication and generate anxiety.For now, investigators are examining possibilities ranging from independent hoaxers and extremist sympathisers to a wider hybrid operation, but there is no publicly verified evidence establishing that Moscow or any state-backed organisation directed the campaign.You use AI every day. articles.title: Winter support for Wolverhampton residents facing cost-of-living pressure
articles.summary: The plans aim to help more people access food, financial advice and help with heating costs.
articles.body:
Plans have been announced to help more people access affordable food, financial advice and help with heating costs this winter.

New community shops are due to open in Pendeford and Graiseley and a shop in Bilston is set to reopen. About 17,000 people have used Wolverhampton's network of community shops over the past six months, said City of Wolverhampton Council.

But council leader Stephen Simkins said many residents still faced difficult choices over household bills. "We know times are still tough for many residents," he added.

The council said more than 135,000 people have received support through its cost-of-living programmes, while more than £18.5m has been distributed to residents.

Simkins said: "Our ambition is simple, we want Wolverhampton to be a city where everyone has the opportunity to live a safe, secure and happy life.

"This winter, we will protect the most vulnerable and ensure nobody is left behind."

The new measures have been announced alongside the launch of a new three-year financial wellbeing strategy to support residents struggling with living costs.

About three tonnes of food are redistributed each month through weekly community markets, with plans to expand the scheme during the winter.

The authority is also extending its Community Chefs programme into schools.

More than 1,000 people have taken part in the initiative in the past six months, producing about 6,000 meals, said the council.

The Boost financial wellbeing service, launched in January to help residents reduce costs and manage household budgets, will also be expanded through the winter.

The council said winter warm packs have already been distributed through the city's family hubs, while adult social care teams are working with health services to help reduce seasonal pressures on the NHS.

articles.title: Former Spice Girls star Geri Halliwell and ex-Red Bull F1 boss Christian Horner get approval to keep oak pergola at their £9.2 million Oxfordshire home despite neighbour complaints over fairy lights and construction noise
articles.summary: Geri Halliwell and Christian Horner are facing fresh objections from neighbours over developments at their £9.2 million Oxfordshire country home, despite
articles.body: Geri Halliwell and Christian Horner are facing fresh objections from neighbours over developments at their £9.2 million Oxfordshire country home, despite securing council approval to retain an oak-framed pergola that had previously been refused retrospective planning permission. The decision has reignited tensions with local residents, who have accused the couple of disregarding planning regulations after fairy lights appeared on the garden structure. Neighbours have also raised concerns about construction noise, changes to the surrounding landscape and the scale of other developments on the Grade II-listed estate. Meanwhile, the planning position of a separate oak-framed gazebo remains unclear.Why did Geri Halliwell and Christian Horner's pergola spark controversyThe former Spice Girl and the ex-Red Bull Formula One team principal attracted criticism after installing an oak-framed pergola and a gazebo in the garden of their Oxfordshire home without submitting planning applications. According to the Daily Mail, the couple's building work had already caused tensions with local residents, particularly because of concerns about the appearance of the structures and their effect on the surrounding area.Neighbours claimed that the developments were affecting the tranquillity of their village and interrupting an unspoilt view of a nearby church. They also raised concerns after fairy lights were wrapped around the pergola, accusing the couple of showing disregard for planning regulations. Some residents questioned whether the couple were receiving different treatment from the local council because of their public profile.How did Geri Halliwell and Christian Horner win approval for their oak pergolaDespite the earlier refusal of retrospective planning permission, the couple submitted a fresh application for the pergola in January 2026. The local council approved the proposal on March 16, allowing the structure to remain within the grounds of their Grade II-listed property. The decision was based on the pergola's siting, scale and design, which planners considered compatible with the existing buildings in the area.The planning official said the proposal would provide adequate standards of amenity and privacy for neighbouring properties. The council's heritage response also supported the design, explaining that the oak-framed pergola, when covered with planting such as wisteria, represented a traditional garden feature that could be sympathetic to the character of the site. Although metal had historically been more typical for pergolas, the wooden structure was considered capable of integrating into its surroundings without causing harm, provided it remained appropriately screened.The council's decision followed complaints from residents who had objected to the structures. One neighbour, who requested anonymity, accused the couple of continuing to use the pergola and gazebo despite the earlier refusal of retrospective planning permission. They particularly criticised the use of fairy lights on the pergola, claiming it demonstrated a lack of consideration for the planning process.The neighbour told the Daily Mail: "The pergola and wooden gazebo that were refused in retrospective planning permission still exist, and are being used with fairy lights on top."They added: "If that is not rubbing our noses in it and showing complete disregard for the planning permission I don't know what is."The same resident also argued that ordinary homeowners would have faced different consequences, saying: "Any ordinary person would have been forced to tear it all down."The neighbour further claimed that the situation highlighted "the level of injustice and inequality shown between the super wealthy and the average person".What did neighbours say about the fairy lights on the controversial pergolaIn the fresh planning application, a representative for Halliwell and Horner defended the design of the structure, describing the oak-framed pergola with integrated planting as a modest addition intended to preserve the character of the property. The plans were drawn up by Riach Architects, with the design intended to ensure that the structure remained subordinate to the main house and did not harm its historical significance or setting.The application also explained that climbing plants would be introduced around the pergola to soften its appearance over time and reduce its visual impact. The representative said the approach responded directly to planning advice seeking better integration with the surrounding landscape. The structure was also positioned to avoid affecting the fabric of the listed house and required minimal ground intervention.The couple's representative described the pergola as a reversible structure that would preserve the long-term integrity of the heritage property while allowing the garden to be used practically. The application concluded that the proposal represented a modest and sympathetic intervention that preserved the character and setting of the house and complied with local and national planning policies.Why has the couple's Oxfordshire property faced repeated planning disputesThe pergola dispute is part of a longer series of planning applications and disagreements involving the couple's property. Their home has previously been the subject of several development proposals, including a first-floor extension, a replacement barn and a new greenhouse, all of which received council approval three years before the latest pergola decision.Last year, the couple were also granted permission to construct a second swimming pool on the grounds, despite objections from residents who feared it would become a "blot on the landscape". The pergola itself is situated near a previously approved swimming pool and consists of an open-framed oak beam structure. The gazebo was also constructed using oak supporting beams and features a pyramidal slate roof.The couple are also awaiting a decision on an application to build a horse walker at their stables. They own a horse-racing company called OMBI, and the proposed development is another planning matter currently being considered by the council.What complaints have residents raised about Horner's country estateBeyond the pergola and gazebo, some neighbours have expressed frustration over the number and scale of developments taking place at the property. Residents have described the projects as "industrial sized" and argued that they do not reflect the purpose of a conservation area.One resident told the Daily Mail: "The local village is not better for it in many ways and there are many disgruntled residents. The noise levels of construction are on a daily basis."The resident also said: "It would be fair to say the landscape is no richer for the input of Mr Horner."Other complaints included claims that public footpaths were being "swallowed up" and concerns about oversized barns, reduced hedges, horse jumps and horse barriers. Residents also raised objections to noisy quad motorbikes being driven around the couple's land, which they said disturbed people living nearby.While the council has now approved the latest application for the pergola, the wider disagreements surrounding development at the property continue. The gazebo's planning position remains unclear, while the application for the proposed horse walker is still being considered.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 3 foreign nationals allegedly used AI to mimic CEOs in $129M scheme, DOJ says
articles.summary: Three foreign nationals have been charged in connection with an alleged international fraud scheme that federal prosecutors say used AI technology to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys and steal more than $129 million.
articles.body: Three foreign nationals have been charged in connection with an alleged international fraud scheme that federal prosecutors say used AI technology to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys and steal more than $129 million. According to an indictment filed in the Southern District of New York, Jacob Soall, who went by “Rocky Balboa” and “Seba Clarke,” was arrested in Spain in June; Sharon Hazan, who used the nicknames “Superman Cash,” “Impossible Mission,” “Fat Boy” and “Ron,” was arrested in Spain in August; and Guy Sheetrit was arrested in the United Kingdom in September. All three are accused of participating in a scheme that ran from July 2024 to February 2026 involving the use of artificial intelligence to impersonate the voices and images of corporate executives and attorneys at major law firms to trick employees of several companies into transferring large sums of money to bank accounts controlled by the group, according to a press release from the U.S. attorney’s office. The trio and their co-conspirators would tell these employees — typically in accounting departments — they needed help with a confidential financial transaction and would use AI technology to mimic the company CEO’s voice, according to the press release. Then, while pretending to be the CEO, they would tell employees to contact attorneys at large international law firms who they said were also working on the transactions, but in reality, those “attorneys” were also part of the scheme, prosecutors said. Finally, one of the people involved in the scheme would instruct the employee to wire large amounts of money to bank accounts set up worldwide, according to the press release. Once the employee wired the money, the group would convert the cash into cryptocurrency “in an attempt to conceal the source, ownership, and control of the stolen proceeds and distribute it amongst themselves and their co-conspirators,” prosecutors said. The U.S. attorney’s office alleges the scheme stole more than $129 million from companies worldwide, including an investment bank in New York, a hospital system in Missouri, a bank in Rhode Island, a hospital system in California, a financial technology company in the U.K., a mutual fund company in Massachusetts and a pet food company in Florida. Soall, from Spain and the U.K., impersonated U.K. attorneys and used a script titled “Lawyer Call” to make himself seem like a real attorney when speaking with victims, the release said. Hazan, from Israel, laundered the money from the scheme, according to the press release. Prosecutors allege that Hazan “boasted that he had been laundering money since 1994; that he had laundered over $400 million in just the past three years; and that, among professional money launderers, he was ‘number one all over the world.’” Hazan was also convicted of conspiracy to commit bank fraud in the Southern District of New York in 2008. Sheetrit, from Israel and the United Arab Emirates, is also accused of laundering funds, the press release said. All three have been charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, two counts of aggravated identity theft, money laundering conspiracy and two counts of money laundering. Each of the seven charges carries a maximum prison sentence of 20 years. “SI technology offers tremendous potential. But the public should recognize that there are some who seek to use this emerging technology to pursue criminal goals,” U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said in the release, using an abbreviation for super intelligence, the White House’s preferred term for artificial intelligence. “I encourage individuals and the business community to consider how to best protect themselves from the emerging threat of SI-enabled crime.”

articles.title: Meghan Markle’s father arrested in Florida over alleged child sexual abuse material
articles.summary: Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was arrested in Florida on Friday over allegations he possessed child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with minors, the Justice Department announced.
articles.body: Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was arrested in Florida on Friday over allegations he possessed child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with minors, the Justice Department announced. He is charged with one count of possession of child pornography, according to a criminal complaint. Markle made his first court appearance Friday afternoon in Tampa, Fla., arriving in a wheelchair pushed by a deputy U.S. Marshal. U.S. Magistrate Judge Lindsay S. Griffin read him the charges and ordered he be given a copy of the charges, Spectrum News reported. He was released after a bond hearing and will be under house arrest, Telemundo Tampa reported. Markle has been living in a senior care facility in Lakeland after being forced to return to the U.S. from the Philippines when he suffered a stroke and a leg was amputated, according to The Associated Press. The FBI seized around 78 items from two storage units rented by Markle that contain “suspected child pornography,” according to court documents. Items seized include film negatives featuring an adult man with naked “pre-pubescent” girls, and a witness “positively identified the adult man as Markle,” according to the documents. Markle, 82, is expected to make his initial appearance Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida in Tampa, the Justice Department said. “These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law,” First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement. “Working with our Justice Department partners, our agents moved quickly, identified and located the explicit material, and arrested Mr. Markle in Florida,” FBI Director Kash Patel said. His arrest comes weeks after authorities in the Philippines said they were investigating allegations that he kept child sexual abuse images at his home while living there. Authorities in the country later said they had recovered thousands of photos featuring “underage male and females.” Markle, a retired television lighting and photography director, denied the allegations last month, calling them “sick lies.” A spokesperson for the Prince Harry and Meghan, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, declined to comment on the arrest. Buckingham Palace has not responded to a request for comment. In a criminal complaint, the FBI said Markle had rented the two storage units in California since the summer of 2008. One unit had mail bearing the name Thomas Markle and an international driver’s permit with his name, birthdate and a photo appearing to be him. The FBI seized 27 items from one unit and 51 from the other. Some of the film negatives, books and slides seized from them still are being reviewed. At least 18 images made from converted negatives “appeared to constitute child pornography,” according to the complaint. At least two images involved an adult, clothed man and a nude female child, the complaint states. A witness identified the man in the images as Markle, the FBI said. The FBI determined some of the seized film was manufactured in New York, so it would have traveled to California as interstate commerce. Based on background in one photo, the FBI determined the images were taken in a hotel in the Philippines, according to the court document. Meghan said in a statement last month that she was “deeply distressed” by the allegations against her father. Their relationship has been limited and fraught in recent years, with her father not attending her wedding to Harry in 2018 amid widespread media scrutiny. Her statement said that she was previously informed of “disturbing allegations” against him, with British police subsequently confirming she was passed a letter in January 2019 “containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom.” London’s Metropolitan Police force said it had not informed other law enforcement agencies about the allegations in the letter at the time, referring itself to Britain’s policing watchdog over the handling of the allegations. “The breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine,” said Meghan, who said she had chosen to keep her children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, away from her father “for one reason: to protect them.” Harry and Meghan stepped back as working royals in 2020 amid widespread reports of a royal rift, leaving Britain for California. Harry, the second son of King Charles and late Princess Diana, leveled harsh criticism at Buckingham Palace and other senior royals across a series of media interviews and a tell-all memoir, “Spare.” The couple returned to Britain two months ago, with their two children moving to schools in the country.

articles.title: Democrats can’t heal the US-Canada bond Trump destroyed
articles.summary: Neither this congressional election nor a change of president in 2028 is likely to restore the bilateral relationship both countries have until recently considered normal.
articles.body:
Democrats won control of both the Senate and House on Tuesday, and Canadians breathed a sigh of relief. After nearly two years of insults, economic coercion, talk of Canada becoming the 51st state , and the whole “ Lake America ” debacle, their relief is understandable.

But it would be a mistake to think that Canadians are willing to return to the status quo ante — to the pre-Trump Canada-U.S. relationship. Neither this congressional election nor a change of president in 2028 is likely to restore the bilateral relationship both countries until recently considered normal.

The international order that gave rise to that relationship is dying. It took shape and flourished within a system structured around American power: first during the Cold War’s bipolar confrontation, then during the unipolar era following the Soviet Union’s collapse. In both periods, U.S. leadership underpinned unusually close economic, political and security ties.

For Canada, the benefits were substantial. During the Cold War, American strategic power helped secure Canada against the Soviet threat, while Ottawa and Washington developed an increasingly integrated system of continental defense .

After 1991, American dominance allowed Canada to scale back defense spending and helped sustain an open international economy in which it prospered through continental trade and multilateral cooperation. That security and prosperity also created space for Ottawa to punch above its weight as a constructive middle power.

The arrangement was never free of friction, but its underlying logic was clear: Close integration with the U.S. made economic and strategic sense. Ironically, by enabling Ottawa to play an outsized role as a helpful fixer and respected peacekeeper, that integration also allowed Canada to be more distinctively Canadian.

Today, that order is giving way to a more fragmented multipolar world, characterized by renewed great-power competition and the erosion of the architecture of international cooperation. Prime Minister Mark Carney captured this shift at Davos in January when he declared that “the old order is not coming back.”

His point was not simply that Canada could no longer count on an America governed by Trump. The foundations of Canadian foreign, economic and security policy were undergoing an epochal transformation.

Multipolarity complicates Canada’s traditional calculation because it changes the incentive structure in Washington. Confronted by China’s rising power, Russia’s challenge to European security and the erosion of American primacy, the U.S. is reevaluating global commitments, pressing allies to shoulder more burdens , onshoring industrial capacity and treating trade and technology as instruments of strategic competition.

Where Washington once had greater latitude to sustain an open economy and tolerate differences with allies, it now increasingly judges close partnerships by their contribution to strategic priorities. For Canada, dependence on American power consequently carries risks that were less pronounced in the past.

Trump has pursued this adjustment in an especially undiplomatic and confrontational fashion. His tariffs and threats against Canada have made the risks of dependence painfully clear. Yet the broader American shift toward strategic competition, economic nationalism and selective international engagement is not simply a product of Trump’s preferences. It reflects structural realities that will persist long after he leaves office.

That is why Tuesday’s election, whatever relief it brings, will not derail or even significantly delay Canada’s ongoing strategic realignment. Congress can challenge tariffs and encourage a more cooperative bilateral relationship. A post-Trump White House may restore a measure of civility and predictability. And all of that will matter. But neither Democrats nor Republicans can recreate the international order that once made Canadian-American economic integration and strategic alignment seem both natural and optimal.

For Ottawa, the logical response is greater strategic autonomy — not separation from the United States, but the capacity to make more choices without being unduly constrained by Washington.

Geography and history make total rupture unrealistic. The two countries share deeply integrated supply chains, vital infrastructure and a continent whose defense requires close cooperation. Russian and Chinese capabilities, the strategic importance of the Arctic and the intensification of gray-zone competition make that cooperation more necessary, not less. The American market will likewise remain indispensable to Canadian prosperity.

Strategic autonomy must operate within those constraints. The objective is not some sort of fortress Canada or a profound rupture of the Canada-U.S. relationship. Rather, in keeping with Prime Minister Carney’s strategy of “value-based realism,” the goal is to diversify trade where practical, strengthen Canadian defense-industrial capacity , build sovereign capabilities and enhance partnerships in Europe and the Indo-Pacific. These are means of increasing Ottawa’s freedom of action.

Tuesday’s election may make the Canada-U.S. relationship less contentious, but it cannot reverse the overall trajectory of that relationship. Canada and the U.S. are both adapting to the emergence of a new geopolitical ecosystem — one which is generating new interests, incentives and anxieties in both capitals.

For Ottawa, greater strategic autonomy was never merely a response to Trump. It is a rational adaptation to this new ecosystem. Whoever governs in Washington, that reality is not going away.

Andrew Latham is a professor of international relations at Macalester College in Saint Paul, Minn., a senior fellow at the Institute for Peace and Diplomacy, and a non-resident fellow at Defense Priorities in Washington.

articles.title: US prosecutor who led Trump-backed election probe exits Justice Department
articles.summary: Jason Reding Quinones’ resignation comes as administration braces for Democrat-led investigations.
articles.body:
Another top prosecutor has resigned from the United States Department of Justice (DOJ) following the Democratic victory in the midterm elections .

US Attorney for the Southern District of Florida, Jason Reding Quinones, submitted his resignation on Friday, according to Attorney General Todd Blanche.

Quinones, a Trump loyalist, had overseen and expanded a federal government probe into Russia’s alleged support for Trump’s 2016 election campaign. While a special investigator later determined there had been no direct collusion between the Trump campaign and Russia, the president has long touted the probe as evidence of a political “witch-hunt”.

Critics have accused the DOJ of pursuing politically motivated investigations at the behest of Trump, who has repeatedly called for retribution against former officials.

Three former officials – former CIA director John Brennan, former Director of National Intelligence James Clapper and former FBI Director James Comey – were reportedly subpoenaed as part of the investigation, although no one has been charged.

Comey was separately indicted over a social media post prosecutors alleged was a threat against the president in April, with court filings suggesting the DOJ is separately seeking to prosecute Comey for allegedly leaking classified information.

A judge dismissed an earlier case against Comey in November of last year. Comey has said the efforts to prosecute him would “almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice”.

Quinones also oversaw the US indictment of 94-year-old Cuban revolutionary Raul Castro, amid a wider Trump administration pressure campaign against the Communist-led nation.

“We ⁠⁠are grateful for Jason’s leadership in combatting violent crime, drug trafficking, sex trafficking, and transnational ‌‌crime, including the indictment of Raul Castro,” Blanche wrote of Quinones in his post on Friday.

The resignation comes just a day after Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the DOJ’s civil rights division, left her post .

Also a Trump ally, Dhillon had been accused of gutting the division, which enforces anti-discrimination laws. She was strongly criticised for reportedly instructing staff not to investigate the killing of two US citizens by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis earlier this year.

On Friday, John Eisenberg, the assistant attorney general in charge of the DOJ’s national security division, also submitted his resignation, according to Blanche.

“He has served with distinction, strengthening our nation’s ability to address threats, both foreign and domestic,” the attorney general said.

The DOJ exodus comes as Trump administration officials are bracing for a slew of new congressional investigations after Democrats won sweeping control of the US House of Representatives and Senate on Tuesday.

The victories will give the party investigative and oversight powers in Congress, including subpoena power. Several probes are expected to focus on the alleged politicisation of the Justice Department.

articles.title: Trump’s latest Ukraine offer may only tempt Putin to step up his war
articles.summary: Kushner and Trump’s talk of a deal may signify nothing. But it may tempt Russia’s leadership to take yet more foolhardy risks.
articles.body: The ‘Shell Bay format’ is an unlikely phrase for history to digest. Named after a 150-acre golf course and luxury residential complex owned by Steve Witkoff, it appeared Thursday as the moniker for the next phase of the Trump administration’s effort to end the biggest conflict in Europe since the 1940s. Witkoff’s fellow peace-envoy and property magnate, Jared Kushner, used the term in a ponderous X post on Thursday, in which he suggested a wide-ranging peace deal was needed in Europe. “For more than 30 years, Europe and Russia have struggled to establish a sustainable security framework,” he wrote. President Trump bolstered the idea after meeting Moscow’s envoy Kiril Dmitriev at the White House, suggesting Thursday. “I can’t tell you what I discussed. But I’m just telling you, it’s going to be a big agreement,” he said. “It’s going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe.” Three European officials contacted by CNN Friday morning did not know what Kushner or Trump were referring to. Speaking to CNN’s Jack Tapper on Friday, Ukraine’s President Zelensky said he knew few details of the proposal and warned it would not be simple. Kushner’s post extolled five key goals: “permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.” It said NATO would be key, even if the above seems to suggest a smaller role for the alliance the United States is the irreplaceable, founding member of. Kushner’s ambitious word-salad did not mention Russia’s invasion of two of its neighbours and two wars with Chechnya in that same post-Soviet period. Moreover, it seemed to suggest any deal would complement NATO, rather than undermine its reason for being. Top NATO and European officials have been meeting in Brussels in the past 72 hours to discuss economic and security concerns around Ukraine, ahead of US-led talks between Russia and Ukraine next week in Abu-Dhabi. There, the US will try and re-ignite discussions on resolving the conflict. Moscow has sent Vladimir Medinsky to lead its delegation, a diplomat fond of historical lectures, whose appointment has led many to think the Kremlin seeks to turn the clock back to May 2025, when the last such talks were held. In truth, months of discussions in Miami, Abu Dhabi, Alaska, Istanbul and Geneva have proven only one thing: Moscow wants its war goals satisfied before it’ll end the war. But the “Shell Bay format” - not a ‘company’, ‘game’, but a bay - emerges at a time when Trump, crestfallen and wounded after the mid-terms, will soon face greater obstacles in his domestic agenda, and perhaps seek to forge his legacy in foreign policy, where he is less restrained. Iran is a less likely candidate for defiant action, given how Trump and many top Republicans blame the war for this week’s electoral drubbing. A form of peace in Ukraine is perhaps a sweeter alternative, and maybe Trump sees, through his ongoing rapprochement and sympathy with Russian President Vladimir Putin, a way he can truly reshape the world, enrich a choice few Americans, and get the US out of bolstering cumbersome European security. It is telling Trump met only with Russian envoy Dmitriev, despite both Kyiv and Moscow dispatching delegations to the White House to meet with the First Lady Thursday. The English-speaking, slick investor has been pushing a variety of possible business deals as the accompaniment to improving Russian-US relations, and Democrat investigators have questioned whether Trump’s inner circle may benefit from these. The sudden return of Ukraine to Trump’s agenda has quickened pulses in European capitals. One European official told me: “we will inevitably see Trump focus on Ukraine now the mid-terms have spoken.” Most are clear-eyed about how any deal cannot simply be imposed on Ukraine - or Europe – without their consent. “Ukraine’s need for European partners (during and post-war) is greater than being forced into accepting a Russian settlement, even if Trump tries to push that”, the official said. The risk is to morale and the mood-music of Trump’s last 18 effective months in office. The winter ahead for Ukraine – beset already in Kyiv by water, cellphone and power cuts – may be prey to further unexplained limits on US intelligence and technical assistance, as we have seen over earlier months. Europe may face heightened sabotage and grey-zone provocations from Moscow. The risk is not that non-American NATO and Ukraine suddenly fold or accept limits to their defense. If history is any guide, 18 months is truly a short period of time, in terms of Russian diplomatic schedules, to enact any sort of deal. What this period of possible US-Russian rapprochement threatens could be more dangerous: that Putin may interpret a US refusal to come to Europe or Ukraine’s aid, as another reason to escalate and ruthlessly pursue the battlefield result from his war of choice that five years of invasion and two years of Trump have failed to bring him. Kushner and Trump’s talk of a deal may signify nothing. But it opens a brief window of heightened opportunity to an increasingly strained Kremlin. And that may tempt Russia’s leadership to take yet more foolhardy risks.

articles.title: Italian chef fired after refusing to put pineapple on pizza, calling it 'insult to his culture'
articles.summary: An Italian chef in Australia was fired from a restaurant after repeatedly refusing to make ham-and-pineapple pizza, calling it an "insult to his culture."
articles.body: An Italian chef in Australia was fired after refusing to put pineapple on pizza, calling the controversial topping an "insult to his culture," according to a labor dispute group's report. Davide Tamburella was fired from La Costa restaurant in Brisbane in May after management raised several workplace concerns, including his refusal to prepare ham-and-pineapple pizzas for customers, according to a ruling from Australia's Fair Work Commission. Tamburella acknowledged it was the third time in four years he had refused a direction to put pineapple on pizza, according to reports. CAN YOU BRING A BIRTHDAY CAKE TO A RESTAURANT? VIRAL PIZZERIA DISPUTE REVEALS THE RULES The latest dispute reportedly involved a customer who had requested ham-and-pineapple pizzas. Tamburella, however, stood his ground. articles.title: Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster
articles.summary: Prosecutors begin investigating EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people.
articles.body:
European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people last week.

Prosecutors backed by a special unit of Spain's Guardia Civil security force said they were conducting the inquiry at the offices of Adif rail infrastructure authority and rail safety agency AESF.

The 28 October accident on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line was one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century.

It is the second EU fraud inquiry opened into Spain's railways this year, after 46 people were killed on the same line at Adamuz in January.

Last week, a train operated by state-owned operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.

The LZB communication system that monitors the position of trains had gone down, and the Renfe train had been given the all clear to start running at normal speed, even though the Iryo train ahead of it had been unable to restart.

The two accidents nine months apart on the same line have claimed 115 lives and dozens more injuries.

Shock of rail tragedy gives way to sorrow and outrage in politically divided Spain

Spanish transport minister resigns days after deadly train crash

The European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) said on Friday it had begun conducting investigative measures at Spain's rail authorities "after the opening of an investigation into possible fraud affecting EU funds allocated to the renovation and upgrading of safety, signalling and communications systems on the Madrid-Seville high-speed railway line".

The EPPO highlighted high public interest in the case, but said no further details would be made public.

As part of the process, a Spanish judge assigned to the case has to ensure the investigation complies with legal safeguards, including authorising any measures that might involve house searches or phone-tapping.

The Urda disaster has damaged the Socialist-led government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez ahead of a 29 November general election and the party is trailing the conservative People's Party (PP) in most opinion polls.

Close Sánchez ally Óscar Puente resigned this week as transport minister, after seeing two deadly accidents on his watch this year.

The PP and far-right Vox say Puente's resignation is not enough and they have demanded that Sánchez resign too.

Many people in Spain have now become wary of taking the train, with reports of widespread cancellations and empty station platforms.

A funeral for the 69 victims at Urda will take place on Tuesday at Toledo cathedral, in the same province that the disaster happened.

Puente's successor, Carlos Cuerpo, has vowed to take all necessary measures to "restore the confidence of Spaniards in our high-speed rail".

Cuerpo met survivors of January's Adamuz disaster on Friday and they handed him a list of 11 demands for improving safety on Spain's railways.

articles.title: MICHAEL RUIZ: California prosecutors revolt after Newsom orders state's worst killers off death row
articles.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom's blanket clemency for 548 death row inmates draws outrage from prosecutors, including in the Gabriel Fernandez case.
articles.body: Shortly after California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced his plans for clemency for hundreds of death row inmates in the Golden State, current and former prosecutors from across the state issued shocked responses to his push for blanket commutations. Among those slated to have their frozen death penalties commuted to life in prison without the possibility of parole is Isauro Aguirre, the Palmdale man convicted in 2017 of torturing and murdering his girlfriend's 8-year-old son, Gabriel Fernandez, who died in 2013. "It’s horrible," Jonathan Hatami, the deputy Los Angeles district attorney who prosecuted the case, told Fox News Digital. 'BABY KILLERS, COP KILLERS' HAVE AN ALLY IN NEWSOM, MURDERED GIRL'S FATHER SAYS AMID DEATH ROW CONTROVERSY Hatami told Fox News Digital that the governor's decision came without any discussions with Gabriel's family. On X, he reposted his heart-wrenching closing argument from before Aguirre's sentencing. "Death was likely a merciful end to Gabriel’s pain — and that only illuminates the torture and abuse that he really suffered," Hatami said at the time. "When he needed it most, no one was there to hold Gabriel, to love him, to caress him, and to just tell him ‘everything will be alright.’" CALIFORNIA SUED OVER POLICY THAT COULD FREE SERIAL KILLERS AS LACI PETERSON'S FRIEND SOUNDS ALARM Aguirre tortured the child for more than seven months before beating him so severely he died with a fractured skull and broken ribs. The abuse included shooting him with a BB gun, burning his genitals and forcing him to eat cat feces. Prosecutors alleged that Aguirre hated the second-grader because he was gay. Gabriel's mother was also sentenced to prison. "The defendant is not a victim," Hatami said in his closing argument. Aguirre, he said, was "pure evil" and a "coward." NEW YORK BILLS COULD ABOLISH LIFE WITHOUT PAROLE FOR SERIAL KILLERS AND COP KILLERS, CRITICS WARN Among the prisoners who would benefit from Newsom's decision are the state's worst — those who have tortured their victims, like Aguirre, murdered children, gunned down police and even serial killers. The "Scorecard Killer," Randy Kraft, killed 16 men between 1972 and 1983. The "Trailside Killer," David Carpenter, killed seven people on hiking trails between 1980 and 1981. "Yosemite Killer," Cary Stayner, murdered a mother, her daughter, the girl's friend and another woman in 1999. Charles Ng was sentenced to death for his role in the abduction and torture, rape and murder of 11 people between 1984 and 1985, including two infants. "I am not aware of any victims’ family members receiving notice of these commutations from the Governor," San Bernardino County District Attorney Jason Anderson said in his own statement, in which he called Newsom's move "the wrong decision." Newsom, however, wrote in an open letter to state residents that the state "cannot morally kill" them. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us," he wrote — later acknowledging that those who would benefit from his move "caused indescribable suffering to victims, their families, communities, and our state as a whole." Current Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan Hochman, along with counterparts in Orange, Sacramento and other counties, have issued statements noting that they will continue to consider the death penalty on future eligible cases following Newsom's surprise announcement Thursday, noting that his action does not change state law or abolish capital punishment. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X "Every death sentence results from years of legal proceedings, involving juries, judges, and multiple layers of mandatory appellate review," Sacramento District Attorney Thien Ho noted in a statement. "A blanket commutation of all death sentences disregards the individualized facts and circumstances of each case, the careful judicial process that led to those lawful sentences, and the voices of victims who have waited decades for justice." While California hasn't executed a condemned inmate in 20 years, death row inmates have largely been excluded from progressive criminal justice reforms made to lighten sentences on other offenders. CHARLES MANSON FOLLOWER TIED TO SHARON TATE MURDERS GETS RECOMMENDED FOR PAROLE AFTER 55 YEARS IN PRISON "Gov. Gavin Newsom’s commutation of the death sentences of all 548 condemned inmates in California is mercy for the wolves...while inflicting the ultimate act of cruelty on the sheep," Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer said in a statement. The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, led by former Sacramento County District Attorney Anne Marie Schubert, sued to block the new regulations. GOT A TIP? We talk about mass shooters, there's a case out of Fresno that happened in the early '90s where a guy killed 10 people and he pled to life without parole. He would potentially be eligible." articles.title: Why isn’t the PEACE Act law already?
articles.summary: Former Treasury official Gregory P. Wilson argues that Congress must urgently pass the bipartisan PEACE Act to repurpose frozen Russian assets for Ukraine’s military and financial needs amid ongoing warfare.
articles.body:
Ukraine is facing an urgent existential crisis on two inter-related fronts. Militarily, Russia has promised another brutal winter of warfare and daily war crimes without remorse for needless civilian casualties. Financially, despite massive assistance from its allies since 2022, Ukraine faces an estimated $35 billion budget gap as a direct result of Russia’s relentless illegal aggression in Europe.

With President Trump’s appeasement of Russian dictator Vladimir Putin failing to bring Russia into serious peace negotiations, Congress needs to step up its game when it reconvenes and answer a perplexing question that directly addresses Ukraine’s dual threats: Why isn’t the pending PEACE Act of 2025 law already?

The bipartisan bill would help Ukraine meet its existential crisis by mandating the accelerated transfer and repurposing of all frozen Russian funds within U.S. jurisdiction to aid Ukraine and allow it to buy defensive weapons to better protect its citizens and defend civilian infrastructure such as its vital energy grid. No U.S. taxpayer funds would be required.

This strong 53-1 committee vote projects a veto-proof majority vote in the House of Representatives if a vote is scheduled during the lame-duck session. The bill could have easily passed already on the House’s suspension calendar — an expedited voting procedure requiring a two-thirds vote, no amendments, and limited debate.

Given Ukraine’s dire financial and military predicaments, we need an answer to the question of why hasn’t this wildly popular legislation already been enacted into law?

The reason the PEACE Act is not law is the Trump administration’s failure to use these Russian assets to negotiate a desperately needed peace from a position of real strength, not cowardly weakness. It is also a result of the House Republican leadership’s abject failure to act as a co-equal branch of the U.S. government under our Constitution and schedule a vote on this noncontroversial, bipartisan legislation.

Trump’s perpetual excuse has been that he is in the middle of peace negotiations with war criminal Putin . But those negotiations have already failed and, unfortunately, peace is nowhere in sight at this moment.

A related question is how much in frozen Russian sovereign assets is subject to U.S. jurisdiction that could be transferred to Ukraine under the PEACE Act?

In 2024, the U.S. Treasury Department reported to Congress that an estimated $5 billion in Russian central bank reserves are at the Federal Reserve. However, the total amount of all additional frozen funds sitting in American correspondent banks was classified by Treasury without explanation.

While the total amount still remains a public mystery, credible experts estimate the total amount of Russian funds here range from $19 billion to as much as $50 billion out of an estimated $300 billion immobilized globally in 2022. Just think about how that money could help Ukraine if it could close its budget gap and buy U.S.-made Patriot missile defense systems to better protect its citizens and defend its sovereign territory.

Speaking on the House floor during debate on June 4 on a bipartisan Russian sanctions bill the administration opposed, Hill publicly called for House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to schedule a vote. The Speaker still has not done so. Hill then attempted to add the PEACE Act as a bipartisan amendment to this year’s National Defense Authorization Act, but his continuing efforts were ignored twice by the House Rules Committee and, by extension, House Republican leadership.

Last year’s powerful 53-1 committee vote is indicative of a veto-proof House vote and subsequent Senate vote, but only if the Speaker schedules an immediate floor vote over White House illusive objections in light of Ukraine’s immediate plight.

Once enacted, the PEACE Act would not only materially assist Ukraine but also strike a decisive financial blow to Russia’s imperialism and hybrid warfare in the rest of Europe. Russia now is a belligerent on the side of Iran and thus partially responsible for U.S. Armed Forces casualties and destruction of our forward bases and military equipment in the Middle East war. Passing this bill before Congress adjourns for the year would be an overdue signal to our allies and warning to our adversaries.

Congress must reclaim and reassert its constitutional role as a separate and coequal branch of government. It must act now to punish Russia and help Ukraine meet its dual existential threats before the onslaught of another winter of senseless warfare and reprehensible war crimes.

The PEACE Act should already be law by now.

Gregory P. Wilson was a former deputy assistant secretary of the U.S. Department of the Treasury from 1986 to 1989.

articles.title: Bloom skin is the K-beauty trend that derms are happy to see replace glass skin — here’s why
articles.summary: Bloom skin is the K-beauty trend replacing glass skin. Dermatologists explain what it is, how to get it and the products and ingredients they recommend.
articles.body: With all the content available online these days, it can be hard to figure out what’s real and what’s hype. While we don’t always have the answers, we have a direct line to people who do — which is why we present to you our series The Internet Made Me Ask, where we have experts break down the truth about some of the buzziest trends (and questions) on our timelines, like zombie skin cells and how often you really need to wash your makeup brushes. For the past few years, glass skin has been one of the buzziest Korean beauty trends. The goal was a complexion so smooth and reflective that it almost looked lacquered, and getting there often meant a 10-step routine. But a new K-beauty trend is taking over, and it’s less about shine. “Bloom skin” is about skin that looks healthy, plump and softly radiant, like a flower in full bloom rather than a polished mirror. It puts barrier health, hydration and treating real skin concerns ahead of a glossy finish. That’s why the dermatologists I spoke with like it more than glass skin. Below, I explain exactly what bloom skin is, how it differs from glass skin and how to build a routine for it, plus products dermatologists recommend to help you achieve it. What is bloom skin? Bloom skin is a K-beauty trend focused on skin that looks healthy and radiant. “I think we’ve seen in recent years that the beauty trend has been increasingly to make our skin look like glass, so it’s really refreshing to now move into an era where we are finally allowing our skin to just look like skin again,” says Dr. Pearl Ugwu-Dike, a board-certified dermatologist based in New York City. “While glass skin emphasizes an almost mirror-like shine, bloom skin is about looking naturally luminous, hydrated, and healthy without appearing overly glossy.” The key to this look is a strong skin barrier. “The idea is that the glow comes from within, from a resilient skin barrier that is well hydrated and nourished,” says Dr. Jane Yoo, a board-certified dermatologist and Mohs surgeon in New York City. Because the trend puts skin health ahead of a flawless finish, it’s also easier for more people to try. “As a dermatologist, I find that this is a more realistic goal,” says Yoo. “It moves the conversation from ‘perfect, reflective skin’ to skin that actually functions on a daily basis, and that’s especially encouraging for my patients with acne or sensitive skin who never felt glass skin was meant for them.” The best products to help you get bloom skin Bloom skin is about having a few products that support your skin, not about having a big routine. “Ultimately, I think the most beautiful skin usually comes from consistency rather than excess,” says Ugwu-Dike. With that in mind, I asked Ugwu-Dike and Yoo which products you need to get the look — here’s what they recommend. According to Yoo, you should cleanse skin with a gentle cleanser that doesn’t leave it feeling tight after using it. Ugwu-Dike suggests this one from Aestura because the formula has ceramides and fatty acids to support your skin barrier, plus glycerin to hydrate without stripping skin. It’s best for normal, dry and combination skin. Ugwu-Dike recommends this La Roche-Posay moisturizer as a way of keeping skin plump and healthy. “It combines ceramides, niacinamide, and glycerin to support the skin barrier and help maintain hydration,” she says. It has a soft, oil-free texture that absorbs quickly, and it’s fragrance-free, which makes it a good pick for sensitive skin. I’ve used it for years, and it keeps my skin hydrated, even in colder months when my skin is especially prone to dryness. Yoo suggests adding a lightweight serum to your routine for extra hydration and radiance, and this hyaluronic acid essence from Cosrx is a good option. NBC Selected associate SEO reporter Ashley Morris has used this essence for years and says it keeps her skin hydrated and helps even out her skin tone. She massages it into her skin twice a day and says it feels lightweight, absorbs quickly and layers well with her other products. One bottle also lasts her months, she says. Ugwu-Dike and Yoo both say a good sunscreen is a must if you want radiant skin. “It is incredibly important to have UV protection through sunscreen, as we know that UV radiation is one of the driving causes of photoaging,” Ugwu-Dike says. This Round Lab sunscreen earned the top spot on our list of the 100 best sunscreens. It has a lightweight, essence-like texture with a dewy finish, and it’s made with hydrating ingredients like birch sap, hyaluronic acid and panthenol. It’s broad-spectrum SPF 50 and fragrance free. Yoo suggests using a good face mask now and then to help brighten your skin and support skin health. This gel mask from Medicube is made with kojic acid and niacinamide, which help fade dark spots and even out skin tone, plus turmeric extract for antioxidant protection and radiance. It feels cooling, and it slowly turns clear as your skin soaks up the formula. You don’t need to rinse it off either, just pat in any left over essence. How to get bloom skin The good news is that this trend doesn’t require a ton more work than you’re likely already doing in your routine. “In my practice, I tell patients that bloom skin is built on fundamentals, not on adding more steps,” Yoo says. She recommends focusing on these basics: Protect your skin barrier. The barrier is your skin’s outermost layer. It’s made of skin cells held together by natural fats, and it locks moisture in and keeps irritants and bacteria out. When it’s damaged, skin can turn dry, red, flaky or easily irritated — in other words, the opposite of what bloom skin looks like. The most common causes of a damaged barrier are harsh cleansers, hot water and overexfoliating. To keep your skin barrier intact, use a gentle cleanser and don’t overdo it with exfoliants. According to Yoo, a gentle exfoliation once a week is plenty.Keep your routine simple. All you need is a cleanser, a moisturizer and sunscreen. Add a treatment product only if you need one for a specific concern. Bloom skin is about a soft, healthy glow that comes from the skin itself, not from layers of product. Every extra step is another chance for irritation, and an irritated barrier shows up as redness, dryness and dullness, the opposite of that plump, radiant look. A short routine keeps your skin calm and hydrated, and over time that’s what gives you the glow.Wear your sunscreen every day. Yoo calls this non-negotiable. “As a Mohs surgeon, I see the consequences of sun damage every day when I remove skin cancers,” she says. Besides raising your risk of skin cancer, sun damage also causes premature aging, dryness and dullness. Skin care ingredients that help support bloom skin While you don’t need a long list of products to help you get bloom skin, it is smart to pay attention to ingredients in the products you use. “There are a few ingredients that I think do a particularly good job supporting the biology behind that naturally luminous appearance,” Ugwu-Dike says. Most of them focus on hydration and barrier repair. A few do more targeted work on tone and texture. Here are the ones Ugwu-Dike and Yoo recommend: Hyaluronic acid and glycerin: These humectants draw in water and hold it in the outermost layer of your skin, Ugwu-Dike says. That can make skin look more supple and soften fine lines caused by dehydration. Yoo adds that they hydrate without feeling heavy.Ceramides and fatty acids: These lipids help rebuild and maintain your skin barrier and reduce water loss. Ceramides are “part of the mortar that holds our cells together,” Ugwu-Dike says. When your barrier is working properly, skin tends to look smoother, more hydrated and less irritated.Niacinamide: This versatile ingredient supports barrier function and helps with uneven tone and texture. Ugwu-Dike says it’s generally well tolerated.Peptides: They help improve your skin’s condition over time and experts previously told us they can stimulate new tissue production and encourage healing. Vitamin C: It brightens, helps fade pigmentation and offers antioxidant protection.Retinoids: These vitamin A derivatives are among the best-studied ingredients for improving texture and tone, and they support cell turnover and collagen production over time. Both experts say to introduce retinol (a type of retinoid) slowly, especially if you have sensitive skin, because it can be irritating.Centella asiatica (cica) and panthenol: These ingredients soothe irritated or reactive skin, Yoo says. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. Meet our dermatologists At NBC Selected, we work with experts with specialized knowledge and authority based on relevant training and/or experience. We also ensure all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and without undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. Dr. Pearl Ugwu-Dike is a board-certified dermatologist based in New York City.Dr. Jane Yoo is a board-certified dermatologist and Mohs surgeon in New York City Why trust NBC Selected? I am a commerce editor at NBC Selected and a journalist who regularly covers wellness and beauty, among other topics. I have written about how to prevent your nose from getting irritated this winter, how to properly clean makeup brushes and more. For this story, I spoke with two dermatologists about bloom skin. Catch up on NBC Selected’s in-depth coverage of tech and tools, wellness and more, and follow us on Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok to stay up to date.

articles.body: A 7-year-old boy in Ansonia, Connecticut, came up with a simple way to earn money for something he wanted for school: a new pair of sneakers. His effort to save for the shoes caught the attention of Officer Joel Perez, who was serving with the Ansonia Police Department.Police officer returns hours later with Adidas sneakersAfter stopping at Landen's stand and learning about his goal, Perez asked the boy about his shoe size.
